at savne.explanation: "At savne" means "to miss" someone or something that is not here: "Jeg savner min familie" (I miss my family). It is not used for missing a bus. For that, Danes say "Jeg nåede ikke bussen" (I did not catch the bus).

sentence.en: I miss my family.

at se.explanation: "At se" means "to see", and also "to watch": "Jeg ser en film" (I am watching a film). "Jeg kan se, hvad du mener" means "I can see what you mean". "Vi ses!" means "See you!". "At kigge" (to look) is about pointing your eyes at something.

sentence.en: I can't see you.

at se på.explanation: "At se på" means "to look at": "Jeg ser på billedet" (I am looking at the picture). The little word "på" (on) is part of it. Do not mix it up with "at se" (to see) or "at lede efter" (to look for).

sentence.en: I am looking at the picture.

at se tv.explanation: "At se tv" means "to watch TV". Danish uses "se" (to see) where English says "watch", as in "se en film" (to watch a film). "At se fjernsyn" (to watch television) means the same. "Tv" is said as two letters, "te-ve".

sentence.en: I watch TV in the evening.

at sende.explanation: "At sende" means "to send", for example a letter, a parcel or an email: "Jeg sender dig en besked" (I send you a message). The person who gets it comes right after "sender", with no word for "to".

sentence.da: Jeg **sender** dig en besked i aften.
sentence.en: I will send you a message tonight.

at sende en sms.explanation: "At sende en sms" means "to text", or literally "to send an SMS". The person who gets it comes right after "sende": "Jeg sender dig en sms" (I send you a text).

sentence.da: Jeg **sender** dig **en sms**, når jeg er hjemme.
sentence.en: I will text you when I am home.

at servere.explanation: "At servere" means "to serve" food or drinks, for example in a restaurant or for guests at home. "Maden bliver serveret klokken 18" means "The food is served at 6 pm".

sentence.en: We serve dinner at six o'clock.

at sidde.explanation: "At sidde" means "to sit": "Jeg sidder på en stol" (I am sitting on a chair). It is also used for being somewhere for a long time: "Jeg sidder ved computeren" (I am sitting at the computer). To sit down is "at sætte sig" (literally "to put oneself").

sentence.en: He is sitting on the sofa.

at sige.explanation: "At sige" means "to say": "Hvad siger du?" (What are you saying?). "At sige hej" means "to say hi". To tell a story, use "at fortælle" (to tell) instead.

sentence.en: What are you saying?

at sige farvel.explanation: "At sige farvel" means "to say goodbye". "Farvel" (goodbye) can sound a little final. Among friends, Danes more often say "hej hej" (bye bye) or "vi ses" (see you).

sentence.en: I say goodbye to my friend.

at sige goddag.explanation: "At sige goddag" means "to say hello", literally "to say good day". "Goddag" is a polite, slightly old-fashioned greeting. With friends you would normally say "hej" (hi).

sentence.en: I say hello to the neighbor.

at skifte tøj.explanation: "At skifte tøj" means "to change clothes", for example after sport or before going out. "At skifte" on its own means "to change" or "to switch" something, such as "skifte job" (to change jobs).

sentence.da: Jeg **skifter tøj**, før vi går ud.
sentence.en: I am changing clothes before we go out.

at skrive.explanation: "At skrive" means "to write": "Jeg skriver et brev" (I am writing a letter). It also covers typing and texting: "skrive en besked" (to write a message). A writer is "en forfatter".

sentence.da: Jeg **skriver** en besked til min ven.
sentence.en: I am writing a message to my friend.

at skulle.explanation: "At skulle" means "to have to" or "should": "Jeg skal arbejde" (I have to work). There is no "at" (to) before the next word, unlike "to" in English. It is also used for plans: "Jeg skal i skole" (I am going to school). Wanting is "at ville" (to want to).

sentence.en: I have to work tomorrow.

at slappe af.explanation: "At slappe af" means "to relax" or "to take it easy". The word "af" (off) is part of the phrase. "Slap af!" means "Relax!" or "Calm down!".

sentence.en: I relax on the sofa.

at slukke.explanation: "At slukke" means "to turn off" a light or "to put out" a fire. "Slukke lyset" means "to turn off the light". The opposite is "at tænde" (to turn on). For a TV you say "slukke for fjernsynet" (turn off the TV).

sentence.da: Husk at **slukke** lyset, når du går.
sentence.en: Remember to turn off the light when you leave.

at slukke for.explanation: "At slukke for" means "to turn off" something like the TV, the radio, the water or the heating: "Husk at slukke for vandet" (Remember to turn off the water). For a light you just say "slukke lyset" (turn off the light), with no "for". "Slukke en brand" means "to put out a fire".

sentence.en: Remember to turn off the water.

at slutte.explanation: "At slutte" means "to end" or "to finish": "Filmen slutter klokken ti" (The film ends at ten). With "med" (with) it means "to stop doing something": "Jeg slutter med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

sentence.en: School finishes at three o'clock.

at smage.explanation: "At smage" means "to taste", both trying food and having a flavour. "Det smager godt" means "It tastes good" and "Det smager af citron" means "It tastes of lemon".

sentence.en: The food tastes really good.

at smile.explanation: "At smile" means "to smile", and it is used much like in English. "Hun smilede til mig" means "She smiled at me": you smile "til" (to) someone.

sentence.en: She smiles at me every morning.

at snakke.explanation: "At snakke" means "to talk" or "to chat", and it is the everyday word for speaking. "Kan vi snakke sammen?" means "Can we talk?". "At tale" (to speak) is a bit more formal.

sentence.en: I speak a little Danish.

at snakke om.explanation: "At snakke om" means "to talk about": "Vi snakker om mad" (We are talking about food). "Om" (about) comes right after it, like "about" in English. It is the casual version of "at tale om" (to talk about).

sentence.en: We are talking about food.

at sne.explanation: "At sne" means "to snow". "Det sner" means both "it snows" and "it is snowing". The word for snow itself is also "sne", as in "Der er sne" (There is snow), so the sentence shows which one is meant.

sentence.en: It snows in Denmark in the winter.

at sove.explanation: "At sove" means "to sleep": "Jeg sover godt" (I sleep well). Going to bed is a different phrase: "at gå i seng" (to go to bed). "Sov godt" means "Sleep well".

sentence.en: The children are sleeping now.

at spille.explanation: "At spille" means "to play" a game, a sport or an instrument: "Jeg spiller guitar" (I play the guitar) and "Vi spiller fodbold" (We play football). It also means "to act" a part. For children playing for fun, Danes say "at lege" (to play).

sentence.en: I play football with my friends.

at spille fodbold.explanation: "At spille fodbold" means "to play soccer" ("football" in Britain). "Spille" (to play) is used for most games and sports. There is no "en" or "et" (a) before "fodbold", just as English says "play soccer", not "play a soccer".

sentence.en: The children play soccer every Tuesday.

at spise.explanation: "At spise" means "to eat": "Vi spiser aftensmad" (We eat dinner). "At spise ude" means "to eat out". For drinking, use "at drikke" (to drink).

sentence.en: We eat dinner at six o'clock.

at spørge.explanation: "At spørge" means "to ask" a question: "Jeg spørger ham om vejen" (I ask him about the way). To ask for something you want, use "at bede om" (to ask for): "Jeg beder om en kop kaffe" (I ask for a cup of coffee).

sentence.en: I want to ask the teacher for help.

at spørge om.explanation: "At spørge om" means "to ask about" or "to ask for": "spørge om vej" (ask for directions) and "spørge om hjælp" (ask for help). "Må jeg spørge dig om noget?" means "May I ask you something?".

sentence.en: I ask for directions.

at spørge om vej.explanation: "At spørge om vej" means "to ask for directions". Danish puts no word for "the" or "a" before "vej" (way) here. A useful question is "Undskyld, hvor er banegården?" (Excuse me, where is the station?).

sentence.en: I asked for directions to the railway station.

at starte.explanation: "At starte" means "to start", for people and for machines: "Bilen starter ikke" (The car won't start) and "Vi starter i morgen" (We start tomorrow). "At begynde" (to begin) means almost the same.

sentence.en: We start on Monday.

at stave.explanation: "At stave" means "to spell": "Kan du stave det?" means "Can you spell that?". It is useful when you give your name over the phone.

sentence.en: Can you spell your name?

at stille uret.explanation: "At stille uret" means "to set the clock", and you use it when the clocks change in spring and autumn. "Stille" means "to set" here. You say which way: "stille uret en time frem" (set the clock an hour forward) or "en time tilbage" (an hour back).

sentence.da: I weekenden skal vi **stille uret** en time tilbage.
sentence.en: This weekend we have to set the clock back an hour.

at stoppe.explanation: "At stoppe" means "to stop": "Bussen stopper her" (The bus stops here). With "med at" it means "to quit doing something": "Jeg stopper med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

sentence.en: The bus stops at the station.

at studere.explanation: "At studere" means "to study", especially at a university: "Jeg studerer historie" (I study history). For studying at home for a test, Danes often say "at læse til en eksamen" (literally "to read for an exam").

sentence.en: She studies medicine in Aarhus.

at stå.explanation: "At stå" means "to stand", but Danish uses it more widely than English: things that are upright "står", such as a bottle on a table. "Der står noget på skiltet" means "Something is written on the sign". "At stå op" means "to get up".

sentence.en: The car is standing in front of the house.

at stå i kø.explanation: "At stå i kø" means "to stand in line" (or "to queue"): "Jeg står i kø i supermarkedet" means "I am standing in line at the supermarket".

sentence.en: We are standing in line for the cinema.

at stå op.explanation: "At stå op" means "to get up" out of bed, literally "to stand up". In the "I have" form Danish uses "er" (am) instead of "har" (have): "Jeg er stået op" (I have got up). To stand up from a chair, Danes say "at rejse sig" (to stand up).

sentence.en: I get up at seven o'clock.

at stå på ski.explanation: "At stå på ski" means "to ski", literally "to stand on skis". Water skiing works the same way: "at stå på vandski" (to water ski). There is no "en" or "et" (a) before "ski".

sentence.da: Vi **står på ski** i Norge hver vinter.
sentence.en: We ski in Norway every winter.

at svare.explanation: "At svare" means "to answer" or "to reply". You answer a question with "svare på et spørgsmål" (to answer a question), and the answer itself is "et svar". Its natural partner is "at spørge" (to ask).

sentence.en: She answers all my messages.

at svømme.explanation: "At svømme" means "to swim": "Jeg svømmer i havet" (I swim in the sea). For a casual dip, Danes often say "at bade" (to bathe, to go for a swim).

related.en: to bathe / go for a swim

sentence.en: The children are swimming in the pool.

at synes.explanation: "At synes" means "to think", in the sense of having an opinion: "Jeg synes, det er godt" (I think it is good). Use it for tastes and views, while "at tro" (to believe, to guess) is for guesses about facts. "Hvad synes du?" means "What do you think?".

sentence.da: Jeg **synes**, det er en god ide.
sentence.en: I think it is a good idea.

at synge.explanation: "At synge" means "to sing". The song itself is "en sang" (a song), and "en sanger" is a singer.

sentence.en: She sings a beautiful song.

at sælge.explanation: "At sælge" means "to sell". It is the opposite of "at købe" (to buy). On shop signs you will see "Til salg", which means "for sale".

sentence.en: They sell fresh bread in the shop.

at sætte.explanation: "At sætte" means "to put" or "to place" something so that it sits or stands, like a cup on a table: "Jeg sætter koppen på bordet" (I put the cup on the table). Do not mix it up with "at sidde" (to sit), which describes where you already are. "Sæt dig" means "Sit down".

sentence.en: I put the cup on the table.

at sætte sig.explanation: "At sætte sig" means "to sit down": the movement of taking a seat. The little word "sig" (oneself) always stays with it, and it becomes "mig" (myself) when you talk about yourself. To say you are already sitting, use "at sidde" (to sit).

sentence.en: I sit down at the table.

en salat.explanation: "En salat" means "a salad" and also "lettuce", so the situation tells you which one is meant. On a menu a side salad is often "en grøn salat" (a green salad).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en **salat** til frokost.
sentence.en: I would like a salad for lunch.

en sandal.explanation: "En sandal" means "a sandal", one open shoe for warm weather. The word is almost the same as in English, and since you wear two, you will often see it with "sandaler" (sandals).

sentence.da: Min ene **sandal** er gået i stykker.
sentence.en: One of my sandals has broken.

en sandwich.explanation: "En sandwich" means "a sandwich", usually a closed one with a filling that you eat with your hands, often from a cafe. A traditional Danish lunch is "smørrebrød" (an open sandwich with no top slice of bread).

sentence.da: Jeg tager en **sandwich** med på arbejde.
sentence.en: I take a sandwich to work.

en seng.explanation: "En seng" means "a bed". Useful phrases are "at gå i seng" (to go to bed) and "at stå op" (to get up, literally "to stand up"). "Jeg går i seng" (I am going to bed) has no "en" in it, just like English has no "a" in "go to bed".

sentence.en: I go to bed at ten o'clock.

en serviet.explanation: "En serviet" means "a napkin". You can ask for one with "Har du en serviet til mig?" (Do you have a napkin for me?). It is said "ser-vi-ET", with the stress at the end.

sentence.en: Do you have a napkin for me?

en side.explanation: "En side" means "a page" or "a side", and also a web page. "På side ti" means "on page ten" and "på den anden side" means "on the other side". "På den ene side ... på den anden side" means "on the one hand ... on the other hand".

sentence.en: Open the book on page ten.

en skadestue.explanation: "En skadestue" means "an ER" (emergency room), where you go for injuries and sudden problems. It is "skade" (injury) and "stue" (room) joined. You say "på skadestuen" (at the ER), using "på" ("on") and not "til" ("to").

sentence.da: Vi kørte på **skadestuen**, fordi han faldt.
sentence.en: We drove to the ER because he fell.

en ske.explanation: "En ske" means "a spoon". "En teske" (a teaspoon) and "en spiseske" (a tablespoon, literally "an eating spoon") are built from it. The plural "skeer" looks odd, but it is correct.

sentence.en: I eat the soup with a spoon.

en skinke.explanation: "En skinke" means "a ham". Danes mostly say just "skinke" for ham on bread or in a meal, for example "et stykke skinke" (a piece of ham) or "brød med skinke" (bread with ham).

sentence.da: Jeg vil have brød med **skinke** og ost.
sentence.en: I want bread with ham and cheese.

en skive.explanation: "En skive" means "a slice", for example of bread, cheese or sausage: "en skive brød" (a slice of bread) and "to skiver ost" (two slices of cheese). For a slice of cake Danes usually say "et stykke kage" (a piece of cake).

sentence.en: I want a slice of bread.

en skjorte.explanation: "En skjorte" means "a shirt" with a collar and buttons. A T-shirt is "en t-shirt", and "en trøje" is a sweater or a top. The "j" in "skjorte" is said like an English "y", roughly "SKYOR-te".

sentence.en: He is wearing a white shirt.

en sko.explanation: "En sko" means "a shoe". The word for more than one shoe looks the same as the single word, so you tell them apart with a number: "to sko" means "two shoes".

sentence.da: Jeg har et hul i min **sko**.
sentence.en: I have a hole in my shoe.

en skobutik.explanation: "En skobutik" means "a shoe store". It is "sko" (shoes) and "butik" (shop) joined into one word, and Danish makes many words this way, so you can often guess new ones.

sentence.da: Jeg skal i **skobutikken** efter nye sko.
sentence.en: I am going to the shoe store for new shoes.

en skole.explanation: "En skole" means "a school". To say that someone is at school, Danes say "i skole" with no "en" or "the": "Børnene er i skole" (The children are at school). For the building, use "skolen" (the school).

sentence.en: My daughter goes to school.

en skov.explanation: "En skov" means "a forest" or "woods". A walk in the woods is "en skovtur" (literally "a forest trip"). For a single tree, use "et træ" (a tree).

sentence.en: We take a walk in the forest.

en skulder.explanation: "En skulder" means "a shoulder". Danish says "the shoulder" where English says "my shoulder": "Jeg har ondt i skulderen" (literally "I have pain in the shoulder") means "My shoulder hurts". "At trække på skuldrene" means "to shrug".

sentence.en: My shoulder hurts.

en sky.explanation: "En sky" means "a cloud". There is also a different word "sky" that means "shy": "Han er sky" means "He is shy". The sentence tells you which one is meant, and "skyet" means "cloudy".

sentence.da: Der er en stor mørk **sky** over os.
sentence.en: There is a big dark cloud over us.

en skål.explanation: "En skål" means "a bowl". The same word, "Skål!", is what you say when you raise a glass, like "Cheers!". For the toast you say just "Skål!", with no "en".

sentence.en: I eat soup from a bowl.

en smartphone.explanation: "En smartphone" means "a smartphone", the same as in English. In everyday talk Danes often just say "en mobil" (a mobile phone), which covers any phone.

sentence.en: My smartphone is almost new.

en smerte.explanation: "En smerte" means "a pain". It is mostly used in the plural: "Jeg har smerter" means "I am in pain". For a pain in one place Danes often say "ondt", as in "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" (literally "I have pain in the head", meaning "my head hurts"). "Smerte" sounds more serious.

sentence.en: I have pain in my back.

en sms.explanation: "En sms" means "a text message", said "es-em-es". It also works as a verb: "at sms'e" or "at sende en sms" (to send a text). For messages in chat apps Danes usually say "en besked" (a message).

sentence.da: Jeg sender dig en **sms** i aften.
sentence.en: I will send you a text message tonight.

en snack.explanation: "En snack" means "a snack", a small bite to eat between meals. The word comes from English and means the same. Another way to say it is "en bid mad" (literally "a bite of food").

sentence.da: Jeg tager en **snack** med i skole.
sentence.en: I take a snack to school.

en sodavand.explanation: "En sodavand" means "a soda", a fizzy soft drink such as cola or lemonade. It is "soda" and "vand" (water) joined into one word. The word for more than one looks the same as the single word: "to sodavand" means "two sodas".

sentence.en: May I have a soda, please?

en sofa.explanation: "En sofa" means "a sofa" or "a couch". Danish says "i sofaen" (literally "in the sofa") where English says "on the sofa", because you sit down into it.

sentence.en: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

en sok.explanation: "En sok" means "a sock". "En strømpe" (a stocking or sock) is the more general word. "Et par sokker" means "a pair of socks", and "Jeg mangler en sok" means "I am missing a sock".

sentence.en: I am missing a sock.

en sol.explanation: "En sol" means "a sun", but you mostly hear it as "solen" (the sun): "Solen skinner" means "The sun is shining". It is also in "solskin" (sunshine) and "solbriller" (sunglasses).

sentence.en: The sun is shining today.

en sommer.explanation: "En sommer" means "a summer". You say "om sommeren" (in the summer, in general) and "i sommer" (this summer). The plural "somre" is shorter than you might guess.

sentence.en: It is warm in the summer.

en sommerferie.explanation: "En sommerferie" means "a summer vacation". It is built from "sommer" (summer) and "ferie" (holiday), and you say "i sommerferien" (during the summer vacation).

sentence.en: We are going to Spain in the summer vacation.

en sovs.explanation: "En sovs" means "a sauce" or "gravy", and Danes use it for brown gravy as well as other sauces. You may also see it spelled "sauce".

sentence.en: The meatballs taste good with brown gravy.

en spisning.explanation: "En spisning" means "a meal" in the sense of an organised event where people sit down together, such as in a club. For an ordinary meal, Danes say "et måltid" (a meal) or just "mad" (food).

sentence.en: The club is holding a dinner tonight.

en station.explanation: "En station" means "a station", a place where trains, metros or buses stop. You say "på stationen" for "at the station". To be clear it is for trains, say "en togstation" (a train station).

sentence.da: Toget kommer til **stationen** om fem minutter.
sentence.en: The train comes to the station in five minutes.

en stegepande.explanation: "En stegepande" means "a frying pan". It is "stege" (to fry) and "pande" (pan) joined into one word. Danes also often say just "en pande" (a pan).

sentence.en: I fry eggs in the frying pan.

en sten.explanation: "En sten" means "a stone" or "a rock" that you can pick up. The plural "sten" looks the same as the singular, so "mange sten" means "many stones". For the material, just say "sten": "et hus af sten" (a house of stone).

sentence.en: There is a stone on the road.

en stjerne.explanation: "En stjerne" means "a star", either in the sky or as a rating. A hotel with "fem stjerner" has five stars.

sentence.da: Vi kan se mange **stjerner** i nat.
sentence.en: We can see many stars tonight.

en stol.explanation: "En stol" means "a chair". It goes naturally with "at sidde" (to sit): "at sidde på en stol" (to sit on a chair). A soft armchair is "en lænestol".

sentence.en: Sit on the chair.

en storebror.explanation: "En storebror" means "a big brother": any brother who is older than you, whatever the age gap. The younger brother is "en lillebror" (a little brother).

sentence.en: My big brother lives in Copenhagen.

en storesøster.explanation: "En storesøster" means "a big sister": any sister who is older than you, whatever the age gap. The younger sister is "en lillesøster" (a little sister).

sentence.da: Min **storesøster** er tre år ældre end mig.
sentence.en: My big sister is three years older than me.

en storm.explanation: "En storm" means "a storm" with strong wind. It is stronger than "blæst" (windy weather) and weaker than "en orkan" (a hurricane).

sentence.en: A storm is coming tonight.

en strand.explanation: "En strand" means "a beach". You say "på stranden" (literally "on the beach") where English can say "at the beach".

sentence.en: We are going for a walk on the beach.

en strømpe.explanation: "En strømpe" means "a stocking" or "a sock". Danes also say "en sok" (a sock), and both words are common. "Strømpebukser" means "tights".

sentence.da: Jeg har et hul i min **strømpe**.
sentence.en: I have a hole in my sock.

en stue.explanation: "En stue" means "a living room", the room where you sit, relax and have guests. It also gives the ground floor its name: "stueetagen" (the ground floor).

sentence.da: Vi sidder i **stuen** og ser tv.
sentence.en: We sit in the living room and watch TV.

en størrelse.explanation: "En størrelse" means "a size", for clothes, shoes or anything else. In a shop you can ask "Har I den i en større størrelse?" (Do you have it in a bigger size?). It comes from "stor" (big).

sentence.da: Har I den i en anden **størrelse**?
sentence.en: Do you have it in another size?

en støvle.explanation: "En støvle" means "a boot", one single boot. You mostly hear "støvler" (boots), because boots come in pairs. "Gummistøvler" means "rubber boots", the kind you wear in the rain.

sentence.en: My left boot is wet.

en suppe.explanation: "En suppe" means "a soup", as in "tomatsuppe" (tomato soup). You eat soup with "en ske" (a spoon), and the verb is "at spise" (to eat), not "at drikke" (to drink).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have **suppen** som forret.
sentence.en: I would like the soup as a starter.

en sweater.explanation: "En sweater" means "a sweater" and is borrowed from English. Danes also say "en trøje" (a sweater, jumper) for the same kind of clothing, and both words are understood everywhere.

sentence.en: I am wearing a grey sweater.

en sygdom.explanation: "En sygdom" means "a disease" or "an illness". It comes from "syg" (sick). You say "Jeg er syg" (I am sick) about yourself, and "en sygdom" for the illness itself.

sentence.en: He has a serious illness.

en sygeplejerske.explanation: "En sygeplejerske" means "a nurse". It is built from "syge" (sick) and "pleje" (to care for). Male nurses are also called "sygeplejerske" in Danish, so the word is not only for women.

sentence.da: Min søster er **sygeplejerske** på et hospital.
sentence.en: My sister is a nurse at a hospital.

en sø.explanation: "En sø" means "a lake", a body of fresh water with land all around it. Do not mix it up with "et hav" (a sea), which is much bigger and salty.

sentence.en: We swim in the lake in the summer.

en søn.explanation: "En søn" means "a son". The letter "ø" does not exist in English; it sounds a bit like the vowel in "bird" without the r. The word for a daughter is "en datter".

sentence.en: My son goes to school.

en søster.explanation: "En søster" means "a sister". "En storesøster" is a big (older) sister and "en lillesøster" is a little (younger) sister. "Søskende" means "brothers and sisters" together.

sentence.en: My sister is a teacher.

et sekund.explanation: "Et sekund" means "a second", a unit of time. Do not mix it up with "second" as in "number two", which is "anden" or "andet". "Et øjeblik" (a moment) is a common way to say that something will only take a short while.

sentence.en: It only takes a second.

et skab.explanation: "Et skab" means "a cupboard", and also a cabinet, a closet or a locker: any closed space for storing things. A word is added to be exact, for example "et køleskab" (a refrigerator).

sentence.en: The plates are in the cupboard.

et skib.explanation: "Et skib" means "a ship", a large boat that sails on the sea. For a small boat Danes say "en båd" (a boat), and for a ferry "en færge" (a ferry). A cruise ship is "et krydstogtskib".

sentence.en: The ship sails to Norway tonight.

et skæg.explanation: "Et skæg" means "a beard". "En mand med skæg" means "a man with a beard". A moustache is "et overskæg", literally "an over-beard".

sentence.en: My father has a long beard.

et soveværelse.explanation: "Et soveværelse" means "a bedroom". It is built from "sove" (to sleep) and "værelse" (room), so it is literally a sleeping room. When describing a home, Danes say how many they have: "en lejlighed med to soveværelser" (an apartment with two bedrooms).

sentence.en: Our apartment has two bedrooms.

et spejl.explanation: "Et spejl" means "a mirror". "Jeg kigger i spejlet" means "I look in the mirror".

sentence.da: Der er et stort **spejl** i badeværelset.
sentence.en: There is a big mirror in the bathroom.

et spil.explanation: "Et spil" means "a game", such as a board game, card game or computer game. It comes from "at spille" (to play), which is also the word for playing music.

sentence.en: Shall we play a game?

et sprog.explanation: "Et sprog" means "a language". Useful questions are "Hvilket sprog taler du?" (Which language do you speak?) and "Taler du engelsk?" (Do you speak English?). "At tale" and "at snakke" both mean "to speak" or "to talk".

sentence.en: Danish is a difficult language.

et spørgsmål.explanation: "Et spørgsmål" means "a question". A polite way to start is "Må jeg stille et spørgsmål?" (May I ask a question?), which literally says "put a question". The word for asking is "at spørge" (to ask).

sentence.en: I have a question.

et sted.explanation: "Et sted" means "a place" or "a spot", and also "somewhere": "Jeg har set det et sted" means "I have seen it somewhere". With other words it gives "ingen steder" (nowhere).

sentence.da: Er der et **sted** at spise her?
sentence.en: Is there a place to eat here?

et stoppested.explanation: "Et stoppested" means "a stop", a place where a bus or tram stops to let people on and off. It is built from "stoppe" (to stop) and "sted" (place). To be exact about a bus, say "et busstoppested" (a bus stop).

sentence.en: The next stop is the railway station.

et stykke.explanation: "Et stykke" means "a piece", as in "et stykke kage" (a piece of cake). In shops it also means "each": "ti kroner stykket" means "ten kroner each".

sentence.en: May I have a piece of cake?

et supermarked.explanation: "Et supermarked" means "a supermarket", a big shop with food and everyday goods. Danes often name the shop instead: "Jeg skal i Netto" means "I am going to Netto" (a supermarket chain).

sentence.en: I am going to the supermarket for milk.

et svar.explanation: "Et svar" means "an answer" or "a reply". "Tak for svaret" means "thanks for the reply". The matching word for answering is "at svare" (to answer), as in "Svar mig!" (Answer me!).

sentence.en: I know the answer.

et svin.explanation: "Et svin" means "a pig", the animal. Calling a person "et svin" is an insult, a bit like "swine" in English. For the meat, Danes say "svinekød" (pork).

sentence.en: The farmer has a pig on the farm.

et sygehus.explanation: "Et sygehus" means "a hospital". It is built from "syg" (sick) and "hus" (house). "Et hospital" means the same and Danes use both words. You say "på sygehuset" for "at the hospital".

sentence.en: He is at the hospital.

et sår.explanation: "Et sår" means "a wound" or "a sore", such as a cut or a scrape. A small cut can be called "et lille sår" (a small wound). You put "et plaster" (a band-aid) on it.

sentence.en: I have a wound on my knee.

salt.explanation: "Salt" means "salt". You do not count it, so you say "noget salt" (some salt) rather than "a salt". The same word also describes taste: "det er for salt" means "it is too salty".

sentence.en: Can you give me the salt?

saltet.explanation: "Saltet" means "salted" and comes from "at salte" (to salt). Do not mix it up with "salt", which describes taste and means "salty".

sentence.en: I like eating salted fish.

samme.explanation: "Samme" means "same" and never changes its ending. It almost always follows "den", "det" or "de" (all three mean "the"). "Det samme" is also a handy reply meaning "the same to you".

sentence.en: We have the same car.

sammen.explanation: "Sammen" means "together". It usually goes after the action word: "Vi spiser sammen" (We eat together). "Alle sammen" means "everyone together", as in "Hej alle sammen!" (Hello everyone!). The opposite is "alene" (alone).

sentence.en: We live together.

sandaler.explanation: "Sandaler" means "sandals". One sandal is "en sandal", but shoes come as a pair, so you mostly hear this "more than one" form.

sentence.en: I wear sandals on the beach.

seks.explanation: "Seks" means "six". It is also the start of "seksten" (sixteen), but "tres" (sixty) is a completely different word.

sentence.en: I get up at six o'clock.

seksten.explanation: "Seksten" means "sixteen". It is "seks" (six) plus "-ten", like "-teen" in English. Do not mix it up with "tres" (sixty), which sounds different.

sentence.en: My daughter is sixteen years old.

selv.explanation: "Selv" has two main jobs. After a person or thing it means "myself", "yourself" or "herself", as in "Jeg gør det selv" (I do it myself). At the start it means "even", as in "Selv min mor ved det" (Even my mother knows it). Do not mix it up with "sig selv", which means "himself" or "themselves".

sentence.en: I make the food myself.

forms.en: Thanks for the help. - You're welcome.

forms.da: Tak for i aftes. - Selv tak.
forms.en: Thanks for last night. - Thanks to you too.

selv tak.explanation: "Selv tak" means "you're welcome". It is the usual answer when someone says "tak" (thanks) to you, and it literally means "thanks yourself". It also works to return thanks: "Tak for i aftes" - "Selv tak" (Thanks for last night - Thanks to you too).

sentence.en: "Thanks for the help!" - "You're welcome!"

selvfølgelig.explanation: "Selvfølgelig" means "of course". It shows that something is obvious or that you gladly agree, as in "Må jeg låne din pen?" - "Selvfølgelig!" (May I borrow your pen? - Of course!). For "of course not", say "selvfølgelig ikke".

sentence.en: Of course you can borrow it.

senere.explanation: "Senere" means "later". It is used for time: "Vi ses senere" (See you later) and "senere i dag" (later today). Do not mix it up with "sent", which means "late": "Det er sent" (It is late).

sentence.en: I will call you later.

sennep.explanation: "Sennep" means "mustard". You do not count it, so you say "noget sennep" (some mustard), as in "Vil du have noget sennep?" (Do you want some mustard?).

sentence.en: I want mustard on the sausage.

sent.explanation: "Sent" means "late", as in not early: "Vi kom sent hjem" (We came home late). Do not mix it up with "senere", which means "later". To say you are running late, say "Jeg kommer for sent" (I am coming too late) or "Jeg er forsinket" (I am delayed).

sentence.da: Det er for **sent** at ringe nu.
sentence.en: It is too late to call now.

september.explanation: "September" means "September", but Danish writes month names with a small letter: "i september" (in September). The same goes for every month, for example "august".

sentence.en: It gets cooler in September.

forms.en: Will we see each other tomorrow?

ses i morgen.explanation: "Ses i morgen" means "see you tomorrow". It is a friendly goodbye when you know you will meet the person again tomorrow. You can swap "i morgen" for another time, like "ses i aften" (see you tonight).

sentence.en: See you tomorrow, and sleep well!

shampoo.explanation: "Shampoo" means "shampoo" and is spelled the same as in English. You do not count it, so you say "noget shampoo" (some shampoo).

sentence.en: Do you have shampoo for me?

shorts.explanation: "Shorts" means "shorts", the same word as in English. It is always used for more than one, as in "mine shorts" (my shorts). You can also say "korte bukser" (short trousers).

sentence.da: Det er varmt, så jeg tager **shorts** på.
sentence.en: It is warm, so I am putting on shorts.

siden.explanation: "Siden" means "since" and also "ago". Since: "siden i går" (since yesterday). Ago: "for to år siden" (two years ago), where "siden" comes last.

sentence.en: I have lived here since 2020.

sidst.explanation: "Sidst" means "last" in the sense of coming after everyone else or at the end: "Jeg kom sidst" (I came last). Before a thing, use "sidste", as in "sidste gang" (the last time). The opposite is "først" (first).

sentence.en: He came last to the party.

sidste.explanation: "Sidste" means "last", both final and most recent: "den sidste bus" (the last bus), "sidste uge" (last week), "sidste år" (last year). The opposite is "første" (first).

sentence.da: Det er den **sidste** bus i dag.
sentence.en: It is the last bus today.

forms.en: She is looking forward to it.

sig.explanation: "Sig" means "oneself" (himself, herself, itself, themselves). It is used when the person doing something is also the one it happens to: "Han vasker sig" (He washes himself). For "I" and "you" Danish uses "mig" (myself) and "dig" (yourself) instead. Many Danish verbs always come with it, such as "at glæde sig" (to look forward).

sentence.en: He washes himself every morning.

sikker.explanation: "Sikker" means "sure" and "safe": "Er du sikker?" (Are you sure?), "Jeg er sikker" (I am sure), "en sikker bil" (a safe car). Before more than one thing it becomes "sikre", not "sikkere": "sikre steder". The opposite is "usikker" (unsure).

sentence.en: Are you sure about that?

sin.explanation: "Sin" means "his own", "her own" or "its own", and goes with en-words. It points back to the person doing the action: "Han ser sin bror" (He sees his own brother). "Han ser hans bror" would mean someone else's brother. For "I" and "you" Danish uses "min" (my) and "din" (your).

sentence.en: She loves her (own) dog.

sine.explanation: "Sine" means "his own" or "her own" when it is about more than one thing: "Han ser sine venner" (He sees his own friends). It points back to the person doing the action, and it is used with both en-words and et-words. For one thing, use "sin" or "sit".

sentence.en: She calls her (own) parents.

sit.explanation: "Sit" means "his own", "her own" or "its own", and goes with et-words, like "sit hus" (his own house). It points back to the person doing the action. If the thing belongs to someone else, use "hans" (his) or "hendes" (her).

sentence.en: He looks after his (own) child.

sjette.explanation: "Sjette" means "sixth". It comes from "seks" (six), but the spelling changes: it is not "sekste". It is used for order and for dates: "den sjette maj" (the sixth of May).

sentence.en: She lives on the sixth floor.

sjov.explanation: "Sjov" means "fun" and also "funny": a party and a joke can both be "sjov". "Det var sjovt" means "That was fun", and "for sjov" means "for fun" or "as a joke". The opposite is "kedelig" (boring).

sentence.en: That was a fun evening.

skandinavien.explanation: "Skandinavien" means "Scandinavia". Place names start with a capital letter in Danish, but "skandinavisk" (Scandinavian) does not. Strictly, Scandinavia is Denmark, Norway and Sweden. When Danes also mean Finland and Iceland, they say "Norden" (the Nordic countries).

sentence.en: Denmark is in Scandinavia.

sko.explanation: "Sko" means "shoes". It looks the same for one shoe and many: "en sko" (one shoe), "mine sko" (my shoes). Danish says "the" where English says "my": "Jeg tager skoene på" means "I put my shoes on".

sentence.en: I have bought new shoes.

skyet.explanation: "Skyet" means "cloudy". It comes from "en sky" (a cloud). The opposite is "solrig" (sunny). In weather forecasts you also hear "overskyet" (overcast), when clouds cover the whole sky.

sentence.en: It is cloudy today.

forms.da: Skynd dig, vi er sent på den.

skynd dig.explanation: "Skynd dig" means "hurry up" and is said to one person. To several people, say "skynd jer". The little words "dig" and "jer" mean "yourself" (one person) and "yourselves" (several people). It is a direct command, so it can sound a bit pushy.

sentence.da: **Skynd dig**, toget går om fem minutter!
sentence.en: Hurry up, the train leaves in five minutes!

skål.explanation: "Skål" means "cheers", said when you raise your glass to drink with others. Add "for" and a name or "dig" (you) to toast someone: "Skål for dig!" It is the same word as "en skål" (a bowl).

sentence.en: Cheers, and happy birthday!

slidt.explanation: "Slidt" means "worn": old and used up from much use, as in "en slidt sofa" (a worn sofa). It is also used about people: "Jeg er helt slidt" means "I am completely worn out".

sentence.en: The sofa is very worn.

slik.explanation: "Slik" means "candy" (sweets). You do not count it and normally use it without "a": "Jeg spiser for meget slik" (I eat too much candy).

sentence.en: Children love candy.

slut.explanation: "Slut" means "over" or "finished", used after "er" (is): "Ferien er slut" (The holiday is over). It also means something has run out: "Mælken er slut" (The milk has run out). "Til slut" means "in the end".

sentence.en: The school day is over.

smal.explanation: "Smal" means "narrow", for streets, paths, doors and windows. It is the opposite of "bred" (wide). It is about width, not about being thin like paper; for that use "tynd" (thin).

sentence.da: Der er en **smal** sti ned til stranden.
sentence.en: There is a narrow path down to the beach.

smuk.explanation: "Smuk" means "beautiful", for people, places, views and things. It is a bit stronger than "pæn" (nice-looking). The opposite is "grim" (ugly). "Hvor er det smukt!" means "How beautiful it is!"

sentence.da: Det er en **smuk** dag i dag.
sentence.en: It is a beautiful day today.

smør.explanation: "Smør" means "butter". It is also the word for putting butter on something: "at smøre" (to spread). "Smør på brødet" means "butter on the bread", and "smørrebrød" is literally "butter-bread", a slice of bread with toppings.

sentence.da: Vil du have **smør** på dit brød?
sentence.en: Do you want butter on your bread?

snart.explanation: "Snart" means "soon": "Vi ses snart" (See you soon). With a clock time it means "almost": "Klokken er snart ti" (It is almost ten o'clock). "Så snart" means "as soon as".

sentence.en: The food will be ready soon.

snavset.explanation: "Snavset" means "dirty", as in "en snavset skjorte" (a dirty shirt). It comes from "snavs" (dirt). The opposite is "ren" (clean).

sentence.en: Your shoes are very dirty.

sne.explanation: "Sne" means "snow". To say that it is snowing, use "Det sner" (It is snowing). It is also part of "en snemand" (a snowman) and "en snebold" (a snowball).

sentence.en: The children are playing in the snow.

sokker.explanation: "Sokker" means "socks". Danish often joins two words into one, so wool socks are "uldsokker", from "uld" (wool) and "sokker".

sentence.en: My socks are wet.

solbriller.explanation: "Solbriller" means "sunglasses", from "sol" (sun) and "briller" (glasses). It is always used for more than one, even for a single pair. "Briller" on its own means glasses you see with.

sentence.en: I have forgotten my sunglasses.

solcreme.explanation: "Solcreme" means "sunscreen", from "sol" (sun) and "creme" (cream). When you talk about it in general, you leave out "a": "Husk solcreme!" (Remember sunscreen!).

sentence.da: Husk at tage **solcreme** med på stranden.
sentence.en: Remember to bring sunscreen to the beach.

solrig.explanation: "Solrig" means "sunny". It describes a day, a place or the weather. The opposite is "skyet" (cloudy) or "overskyet" (overcast).

sentence.da: I dag er det en **solrig** dag.
sentence.en: Today is a sunny day.

solrigt.explanation: "Solrigt" means "sunny". It is the form of "solrig" used with et-words, such as "vejr" (weather): "solrigt vejr". It is also used in "Det er solrigt" (It is sunny).

sentence.en: It is sunny at the beach.

solskin.explanation: "Solskin" means "sunshine", from "sol" (sun) and "skin" (shine). "Der er solskin" means "There is sunshine", a normal way to say that the sun is out.

sentence.en: We are enjoying the sunshine in the garden.

solskinsvejr.explanation: "Solskinsvejr" means "sunny weather", from "solskin" (sunshine) and "vejr" (weather). Its opposites are "regnvejr" (rainy weather) and "gråvejr" (gray weather). Example: "Hvis det er solskinsvejr, tager vi på stranden" (If it is sunny, we go to the beach).

sentence.da: Det er dejligt at gå tur i **solskinsvejr**.
sentence.en: It is lovely to go for a walk in sunny weather.

som.explanation: "Som" means "that", "who" or "which", and also "like" or "as". It joins a describing part to a person or thing: "manden, som bor her" (the man who lives here). It also means "like" or "as": "Jeg arbejder som lærer" (I work as a teacher).

sentence.da: Det er den bog, **som** jeg læser.
sentence.en: That is the book that I am reading.

somme tider.explanation: "Somme tider" means "sometimes". It is the two-word way of writing "sommetider", with the same meaning. "Nogle gange" (some times) is another everyday way to say it.

sentence.da: Jeg er **somme tider** træt om morgenen.
sentence.en: I am sometimes tired in the morning.

forms.en: I sometimes go for a walk

sommetider.explanation: "Sommetider" means "sometimes". It can also be written as two words, "somme tider", with the same meaning. "Nogle gange" (some times) is another everyday way to say it.

sentence.en: Sometimes I take the bike.

sort.explanation: "Sort" means "black", as in "en sort bil" (a black car). The opposite is "hvid" (white). It is also used in "sort kaffe" (black coffee).

sentence.en: She has a black bag.

sov godt.explanation: "Sov godt" means "sleep well", said to wish someone a good sleep, most often at bedtime. "Sov" comes from "at sove" (to sleep) and "godt" means "well". It is often said together with "godnat" (good night).

sentence.en: Good night, sleep well!

spaghetti.explanation: "Spaghetti" means "spaghetti", spelled the same as in English. You do not count it, so you say "noget spaghetti" (some spaghetti). Example: "spaghetti med kødsovs" (spaghetti with meat sauce).

sentence.en: We eat spaghetti with meat sauce.

spanien.explanation: "Spanien" means "Spain". Place names start with a capital letter and have no "the" in front: "i Spanien" (in Spain). A person from there is "en spanier" (a Spaniard) and the language is "spansk" (Spanish).

sentence.en: We are on holiday in Spain.

spansk.explanation: "Spansk" means "Spanish", for things from Spain and for the language. Danish writes it with a small letter. For the language: "Jeg taler spansk" (I speak Spanish).

sentence.en: I am learning Spanish tonight.

spinat.explanation: "Spinat" means "spinach". Like in English it is usually not counted: you say "noget spinat" (some spinach). "Rå spinat" is raw spinach and "frossen spinat" is frozen spinach.

sentence.en: There is spinach in the soup.

sport.explanation: "Sport" means "sport", and you say it without "en" when you mean sport in general. "At dyrke sport" (to do sport) is the usual way to say you practise a sport: "Han dyrker meget sport" (He does a lot of sport).

sentence.da: Jeg ser **sport** i fjernsynet hver weekend.
sentence.en: I watch sport on TV every weekend.

spændende.explanation: "Spændende" means "exciting" or "interesting". "Det lyder spændende" means "That sounds exciting". "Interessant" (interesting) is milder and fits less thrilling things.

sentence.en: It is an exciting film.

stadig.explanation: "Stadig" means "still", for something that is continuing: "Han sover stadig" (He is still sleeping). "Endnu" (yet, still) is similar, but "stadig" is the safe choice for something that keeps going.

sentence.en: He is still sleeping.

stadigvæk.explanation: "Stadigvæk" means "still", for something that keeps going: "Det regner stadigvæk" (It is still raining). It means the same as "stadig" (still), and you will hear both. "Endnu" (yet) is different: "ikke endnu" means "not yet".

sentence.en: He is still sleeping.

stegt.explanation: "Stegt" means "fried" or "roasted", depending on the food. It is used for food cooked in a pan or oven, for example "stegt flæsk" (fried pork). The action is "at stege" (to fry or roast).

sentence.en: I would like fried fish.

stille.explanation: "Stille" means "quiet", "silent" or "calm": "Vær stille" means "Be quiet". For a calm, relaxed person "rolig" (calm) also fits. Do not mix it up with "at stille" (to put or place), as in "at stille et spørgsmål" (to ask a question).

sentence.en: She is very quiet in class.

stop.explanation: "Stop" means "stop", the same as in English: a quick order to halt. Add "lige" (just) to soften it: "Stop lige!" is like "Hold on a moment". The action is "at stoppe" (to stop): "Bussen stopper" (The bus stops).

sentence.en: Stop! I forgot my bag.

stor.explanation: "Stor" means "big" or "large". Its opposite is "lille" (small). It can also mean "grown-up": "Hvor er du blevet stor!" means "How big you have grown!"

sentence.en: It is a big house.

storbritannien.explanation: "Storbritannien" means "Great Britain". It is made from "stor" (big) and "Britannien" (Britain). A person from there is "en brite" (a Briton), and "britisk" (British) describes things. It covers England, Scotland and Wales.

sentence.en: He comes from Great Britain.

stærk.explanation: "Stærk" means "strong", for people, coffee, tea, wind and feelings: "stærk kaffe" is strong coffee. For food it also means "hot" or "spicy". The opposite is "svag" (weak).

sentence.en: He is very strong.

størst.explanation: "Størst" means "biggest" or "largest". It goes with "stor" (big) and "større" (bigger), like English big, bigger, biggest. Used alone it stays "størst": "Han er størst" (He is the biggest).

sentence.da: København er den **største** by i Danmark.
sentence.en: Copenhagen is the biggest city in Denmark.

støvler.explanation: "Støvler" means "boots", more than one. A single boot is "en støvle", and a pair is "et par støvler" (a pair of boots).

sentence.da: Det regner, så jeg tager **støvler** på.
sentence.en: It is raining, so I am putting boots on.

sukker.explanation: "Sukker" means "sugar". You leave out "et" when you mean sugar in general: "lidt sukker" (a little sugar). Sugar in your coffee is "sukker i kaffen".

sentence.en: Do you want sugar in your coffee?

sulten.explanation: "Sulten" means "hungry". You say "Jeg er sulten" (I am hungry), just like in English. "Sult" means "hunger", and the opposite of "sulten" is "mæt" (full after eating).

sentence.en: I am really hungry.

sund.explanation: "Sund" means "healthy" in the sense of good for you, for food, habits or a person. Do not mix it up with "rask" (well, not sick right now): "Jeg er rask igen" means "I am well again".

sentence.en: Fruit is healthy.

sundhed.explanation: "Sundhed" means "health" in a general sense, such as how healthy a lifestyle or a country is. For a person's own condition Danes usually say "helbred": "Han har dårligt helbred" (He is in poor health).

sentence.en: Health is more important than money.

super.explanation: "Super" means "super" or "great". Say "Super!" on its own, or put it before another word to make it stronger: "super god" means "really good". It is casual and friendly.

sentence.en: That is a great idea!

svensk.explanation: "Svensk" means "Swedish", and unlike in English it is written with a small letter. The language is also called "svensk". A Swedish person is "en svensker" (a Swede).

sentence.en: My neighbour is Swedish.

sverige.explanation: "Sverige" means "Sweden". The people are "svenskere" (Swedes), and one person is "en svensker" (a Swede). The language and the word for "Swedish" is "svensk".

sentence.en: We are driving to Sweden at the weekend.

svimmel.explanation: "Svimmel" means "dizzy", the feeling that the room is spinning. You say "Jeg er svimmel" (I am dizzy) or "Jeg bliver svimmel" (I am getting dizzy).

sentence.da: Jeg er **svimmel**, fordi jeg ikke har spist.
sentence.en: I am dizzy because I have not eaten.

svinekød.explanation: "Svinekød" means "pork". It is built from "svin" (pig) and "kød" (meat), so the animal is "et svin" (a pig) and the meat is "svinekød", like English "pig" and "pork".

sentence.en: Danes eat a lot of pork.

svær.explanation: "Svær" means "difficult" or "hard to do". Danes often say "Det er svært" (It is hard). Its opposites are "let" and "nem", which both mean "easy".

sentence.da: Danske ord kan være **svære** at sige.
sentence.en: Danish words can be difficult to say.

svømning.explanation: "Svømning" means "swimming" as a sport or activity. The action is "at svømme" (to swim): "Jeg kan svømme" (I can swim). Danes say "gå til svømning" (literally "go to swimming") for taking regular swimming lessons or training.

sentence.en: The children go to swimming on Mondays.

syd.explanation: "Syd" means "south". It joins other words, as in "Sydjylland" (southern Jutland) and "sydpå" (southwards). Its opposite is "nord" (north).

sentence.en: The birds fly south in the winter.

sydamerika.explanation: "Sydamerika" means "South America". Unlike in English it is one word: "syd" (south) plus "Amerika". North America works the same way: "Nordamerika".

sentence.en: She has travelled around South America.

syg.explanation: "Syg" means "sick" or "ill". "Jeg er syg" is what you say when you cannot go to work or school, and "at melde sig syg" means "to call in sick". The opposite is "rask" (well, healthy).

sentence.en: My son is sick today.

syltetøj.explanation: "Syltetøj" means "jam". It is made from "sylte" (to preserve) and "tøj" (stuff). For jam in general you leave out "et": "lidt syltetøj" (a little jam).

sentence.da: Jeg vil have **syltetøj** på mit brød.
sentence.en: I want jam on my bread.

sytten.explanation: "Sytten" means "seventeen". It is built on "syv" (seven), but the "v" drops out, so it is "sytten" and not "syvten".

sentence.en: He is seventeen years old.

syv.explanation: "Syv" means "seven". The "v" at the end is soft and sounds almost like a short "u". Seventeen is "sytten", where the "v" drops out, and seventy is "halvfjerds", which looks nothing like "syv".

sentence.da: Der er **syv** dage i en uge.
sentence.en: There are seven days in a week.

syvende.explanation: "Syvende" means "seventh". It is used for the order of things and for dates: "den syvende juli" is the seventh of July. In writing you can use "7." with a dot after the number.

sentence.da: Det er min **syvende** uge i Danmark.
sentence.en: It is my seventh week in Denmark.

så.explanation: "Så" means "so" or "then". It can show a result ("Det regner, så vi bliver hjemme": It is raining, so we stay home), a next step ("og så går vi": and then we go) or add strength ("så stor": so big). Careful: "så" also means "saw", as in "Jeg så ham" (I saw him), from "at se" (to see).

sentence.da: Først spiser vi, og **så** går vi hjem.
sentence.en: First we eat, and then we go home.

forms.en: Stay as long as you like

så længe.explanation: "Så længe" means "as long as": one thing is true only while another is. On its own it can also mean "for now" or "in the meantime": "Det er fint så længe" (That is fine for now).

sentence.da: Du må bo her, **så længe** du vil.
sentence.en: You may live here as long as you want.

sådan.explanation: "Sådan" means "like that", "such" or "this way". Said on its own, "Sådan!" is like "There you go!". It also shows how something is done: "Man gør det sådan" is "You do it like this".

sentence.en: You do it like this.

sæbe.explanation: "Sæbe" means "soap". Like in English it is not counted, so you say "noget sæbe" (some soap) or "et stykke sæbe" (a piece of soap). Dish soap is a different word: "opvaskemiddel" (washing-up liquid).

sentence.en: I wash my hands with soap.

sød.explanation: "Sød" means "sweet" in taste ("sød kage", sweet cake) and also "sweet" or "cute" for people, animals and small children. A common phrase is "Det er sødt af dig" (That is sweet of you). The opposite for taste is "sur" (sour).

sentence.en: How sweet she is!

sølv.explanation: "Sølv" means "silver", both the metal and the colour. In sport it is also the second-place medal: "Hun vandt sølv" (She won silver).

sentence.en: My ring is made of silver.

søndag.explanation: "Søndag" means "Sunday", and unlike in English it is written with a small letter. Say "på søndag" for this coming Sunday (on Sunday) and "om søndagen" for every Sunday (on Sundays).

sentence.en: We are visiting my mother on Sunday.
